messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Hopelessness: I have no future, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Ramirez was twenty-six when his younger brother Javier was killed, caught in a stray bullet outside a bodega two blocks from the house they had grown up in. Mateo had been working a double shift at the county detention center that night, and he learned about it from his wife Elena’s voicemail at four in the morning, her voice cracking as she told him to come home. He drove there with his hands shaking on the wheel, certain that if he had not been working, if he had just answered Javier’s last call an hour earlier, he could have kept him inside, could have been there to push him out of the way. That thought had not faded. It had only calcified.

In the months afterward, Mateo found himself moving through his days as though he were watching himself from a distance. During a shift in the housing unit, he would suddenly notice that he could not feel the floor under his boots, or that the inmates’ voices seemed to come from the far end of a tunnel. The feeling was worse when he saw a news report about a shooting or heard the word “loss” spoken by anyone, whether a coworker talking about a family death or a chaplain leading a grief group inside the prison. He would freeze, his chest tightening, and then he would press his palms against his face, covering his eyes and mouth until the moment passed. A couple of times he did it in the control booth, and the officer next to him asked if he was okay. Mateo said he was just tired.

He had come to believe that happiness was a thing he used to have, like a pair of keys he had misplaced and would never find again. At home, Elena would try to draw him into a conversation about the weekend, and he would feel a surge of irritation that had nothing to do with her. He would pick a fight about something small—the way she left dishes in the sink, the volume of the television—and then let the argument escalate until she walked away. The heat of the conflict, the sharp back-and-forth, gave him a few minutes of relief. He could focus on the anger instead of the image of Javier slumped against the brick wall. But afterward, the emptiness was deeper, and he hated himself for it.

Anything that reminded him of his brother had become poison. He removed Javier’s photo from his phone and asked Elena to put away the framed picture from their parents’ house. He stopped driving past the bodega. When his mother called to talk about Javier’s birthday, Mateo hung up without saying goodbye and then ignored her calls for a week. The avoidance had a cost: his mother stopped calling as often, and Elena had started sleeping on the couch three nights out of seven, telling him she could not keep walking on eggshells. Mateo did not argue. He was certain he had no future, that he would always be this hollow version of himself, and that he deserved it. He should have protected Javier. That failure had defined him.

What finally brought Mateo to the clinic was an incident at work. During a routine cell search, an inmate began weeping after receiving a letter about a family member’s death. Mateo stood in the doorway and felt the world tilt. He walked out of the unit, sat in the break room with his hands over his face, and did not return for twenty minutes. His supervisor told him he needed to “sort himself out” or take leave. Elena had said the same thing, with more tears. Mateo agreed to come because he was tired of feeling like a stranger in his own life, and because he was afraid that if he did not change something, he would lose the only person still willing to sit beside him. He did not believe he could feel happy again, but he was hoping, against the weight of everything, that he might at least stop feeling like a failure every single day.
